subject: Biology
title: Organisms and Populations
summary: The chapter studies ecology at the level of the population: what a population is, the attributes it has that an individual does not (birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age pyramid, density), how its size changes through natality, mortality, immigration and emigration, the exponential and logistic growth models, life history variation, and the six interspecific interactions (predation, competition, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism, amensalism) with the NCERT examples for each. It is a short chapter in the rationalised syllabus, and the board tests it through the two growth curves, the three age pyramids, the interaction table and a fixed set of named examples, so it rewards exact recall of NCERT terms.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 12 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper. This chapter is the first of the three chapters in Unit X, Ecology and Environment (Organisms and Populations, Ecosystem, Biodiversity and Conservation), and the unit carries 12 marks in total. Organisms and Populations typically contributes 4 to 6 marks: one or two 1-mark items, a 2- or 3-mark question on an interaction or on population growth, and in recent years either a 4-mark case study on age pyramids or growth curves or a 5-mark question on the growth models.

question_types.note: Identify the interaction from a pair of organisms (orchid on a mango tree, clown fish and sea anemone, cattle egret and cattle, cuckoo and crow, Cuscuta on a hedge, lichen, mycorrhiza), the equation or name of a growth model (Verhulst-Pearl), the meaning of K and r, the shape of an age pyramid, which process reduces population density, the reason the Abingdon tortoise went extinct, what Connell's barnacle experiment shows, the source of the Monarch butterfly's toxin.

Why the logistic model is more realistic than the exponential one; why predators are called prudent; why the female Anopheles mosquito is not a parasite; why the eggs of the cuckoo resemble those of the crow; why the fig can be pollinated only by its partner wasp; why a single banyan tree should be measured by biomass and not by number; why cattle and goats never browse on Calotropis.

Calculate a birth rate, a death rate or the net change in a population from given numbers; name and explain the interaction between two given organisms; state Gause's principle and how recent studies modified it; list two ways to estimate tiger population without counting; give two adaptations of parasites; distinguish ectoparasite and endoparasite with examples; explain brood parasitism; explain sexual deceit in Ophrys; explain why the Abingdon tortoise went extinct.

Draw the three age pyramids and state what each means for growth; draw and explain the exponential and logistic growth curves; explain the four processes that change population density with the equation; explain the roles of predators beyond energy transfer, with the Pisaster and prickly pear examples; explain fig-wasp mutualism; explain competitive release with Connell's barnacles; describe the defences of plants against herbivores; explain resource partitioning with MacArthur's warblers.

Describe the exponential growth model with its equations, the meaning of r, the integral form, the J-shaped curve and Darwin's elephant remark; describe the Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth model with its equation, the phases of the sigmoid curve, the carrying capacity and why it is considered more realistic; a complete account of predation, its roles and the defences of prey; a complete account of parasitism with adaptations, life cycles, ecto- and endoparasites and brood parasitism; the six population interactions with the +/−/0 table and an example of each.

Age pyramids of two countries (Rwanda-type expanding versus Sweden-type stable) with questions on growth status and policy; a graph of two growth curves with questions on which curve shows unlimited resources, what the dotted line K means and which equation describes each; a passage on the Monarch butterfly or Calotropis leading to questions on prey defences; a passage on population figures leading to birth-rate and net-change arithmetic.

Age pyramids: expanding, stable and declining shapes, the three age groups, reading a real pair of pyramids

sections.heading: Introduction: ecology and its four levels
sections.body:
NCERT opens by reminding you of the Class 11 definition: ecology is the study of the interactions among organisms and between the organism and its physical (abiotic) environment. Ecology works at four levels of biological organisation: organisms, populations, communities and biomes. Ecology at the level of the organism is physiological ecology, which asks how an individual copes with its environment. This chapter moves one level up and studies ecology at the level of the population. The next chapter (Ecosystem) works at the community and ecosystem level, and the chapter after it (Biodiversity) at the level of biomes and the whole biosphere.

One line from the introduction is worth memorising because it explains why the whole chapter is built around populations rather than individuals: although an individual organism is the one that has to cope with a changed environment, it is at the population level that natural selection operates to evolve the desired traits. Population ecology therefore links ecology to population genetics and evolution. That sentence is the standard answer to any question that asks why population ecology is important.

A note on the syllabus, because many question banks still carry old questions. The rationalised NCERT chapter (2023 onwards) removed the earlier material on major abiotic factors (temperature, water, light, soil), on how organisms respond to them (regulate, conform, migrate, suspend) and on adaptations such as the kangaroo rat, altitude sickness and desert plants. The current chapter is only about populations: their attributes, their growth, life history variation and the interactions between populations. CBSE sets questions from the rationalised text, so prepare this chapter from the sections below and do not spend time on eurythermal and stenothermal organisms, hibernation or diapause, however often you see them in older papers.
sections.tip: If a question asks 'at which level of organisation does natural selection operate', the answer NCERT wants is 'at the population level', not 'the individual'.

sections.heading: 11.1 Populations: what a population is
sections.body:
In nature, individuals of a species are rarely alone; they live in groups that share or compete for the same resources, and they can interbreed. NCERT defines a population as a group of individuals of the same species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources and potentially interbreeding. The five NCERT examples are worth reproducing exactly, because 1-mark questions ask for two of them: cormorants in a wetland, rats in an abandoned dwelling, teakwood trees in a forest tract, bacteria in a culture plate, and lotus plants in a pond. Each of these is a population. Note that the definition includes plants and microbes as much as animals.

A community is the next level up: an assemblage of populations of different species living together and interacting in a given area. The NCERT exercise asks you to define both terms in one question, so learn them as a pair. A population is one species; a community is many populations, and the interactions between them are the subject of the last section of this chapter.

Why study populations at all? Because a population has properties that no individual has. An individual is born once and dies once; a population has a birth rate and a death rate. An individual is male or female; a population has a sex ratio. An individual has an age; a population has an age distribution. And a population has a size or density. These four are the population attributes of the next section. Whenever the board asks 'list the attributes that a population possesses but an individual does not', these are the four to write, with one line of explanation each.

A second reason is practical. The size of a population is not fixed; it changes with food availability, predation pressure and weather. Knowing how populations grow and how they interact is what lets us manage fisheries, control pests, protect endangered species and plan for a human population. NCERT makes the point that governments introduce restraints on human population growth precisely because no population can grow without limit.
sections.tip: Write 'same species' in the definition of population. A group of animals of different species in an area is a community, and writing 'group of organisms' without the species condition loses the mark.

sections.heading: 11.1.1 Population Attributes: birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age pyramid and density
sections.body:
Birth rate and death rate. These are per-capita rates, not total counts. NCERT's worked example: a pond had 20 lotus plants last year; through reproduction 8 new plants were added, taking the current population to 28. The birth rate is 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year. Notice that you divide by the initial population (20), not the final one (28). The death-rate example: if 4 individuals in a laboratory population of 40 fruit flies died in a week, the death rate is 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week. Every numerical in this chapter is one of these two divisions or the net-change equation of the next section; get the denominator right and state the unit.

Sex ratio. An individual is either male or female, but a population has a sex ratio, for example 60 per cent females and 40 per cent males.

Age distribution and the age pyramid. A population at any time is made of individuals of different ages. If the per cent of individuals in each age group is plotted, the resulting structure is called an age pyramid. For human populations the pyramid shows males and females side by side. NCERT uses three age groups: pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive. The shape of the pyramid tells you the growth status of the population: a broad base with many pre-reproductive individuals is a growing (expanding) population, triangular in shape; a pyramid with roughly equal pre-reproductive and reproductive groups and a narrower top is a stable population, bell-shaped; a pyramid with a narrow base and a wide reproductive and post-reproductive band is a declining population, urn-shaped. Age pyramids of human populations are used by governments for planning: an expanding pyramid means more schools and jobs will be needed; a declining one means more old-age care.

Population size or density (N). Population size, technically called population density and designated N, is the total number (or biomass) of individuals in the population. In nature it may be as low as fewer than 10 (Siberian cranes at Bharatpur wetlands in a year) or run into millions (Chlamydomonas in a pond). NCERT is careful to say that density need not be measured in numbers only, and gives four situations that are examined regularly. (1) If a field has 200 Parthenium plants but a single huge banyan tree with a large canopy, calling the banyan's density 'low' underestimates its enormous role in the community; here per cent cover or biomass is the more meaningful measure. (2) When the population is huge and counting is impossible (a dense microbial culture in a petri dish), total number is not a usable measure. (3) For many investigations, relative density is enough: the number of fish caught per trap is a good enough measure of the fish density in a lake. (4) We are often obliged to estimate population size indirectly, without counting or even seeing the animals: the tiger census in our national parks and tiger reserves is based on pug marks and fecal pellets. The 2-mark question 'name two methods to estimate the tiger population' expects exactly these two.

formulas.expr: Birth rate = number of births in the period ÷ initial population size
where: 8 new lotus plants in a pond of 20 → 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year

formulas.expr: Death rate = number of deaths in the period ÷ initial population size
where: 4 deaths in 40 fruit flies in a week → 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week

sections.tip: Draw the three age pyramids as three separate outlines side by side, each with the three age-group labels on the vertical axis and 'males | females' across the base, and write the growth status under each. The examiner awards marks for the shapes and the labels, not for artistic quality.

sections.heading: 11.1.2 Population Growth: the four processes and the population equation
sections.body:
The size of a population is not a static parameter. It changes with time depending on food availability, predation pressure and weather, and the change can be traced to four basic processes. Two of them add individuals and two remove them.

  • Natality (B): the number of births during a given period in the population that are added to the initial density.
  • Mortality (D): the number of deaths in the population during the given period.
  • Immigration (I): the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during the period under consideration.
  • Emigration (E): the number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and went elsewhere during the period.

Natality and immigration increase the density; mortality and emigration decrease it. If N is the population density at time t, then the density at time t + 1 is

Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) − (D + E)]

Read the equation as a sentence: the population density will increase if the number of births plus the number of immigrants (B + I) is more than the number of deaths plus the number of emigrants (D + E), and otherwise it will decrease. A recent board MCQ gave a rat population in a granary with natality 280, mortality 200, immigration 40 and emigration 50 and asked for the net increase: (280 + 40) − (200 + 50) = 320 − 250 = 70. Always show the two brackets, then the subtraction.

NCERT adds a qualification that turns up as a 1-mark or Assertion–Reason item. Under normal conditions births and deaths are the most important factors influencing population density; immigration and emigration assume importance only under special conditions. The example given is a habitat that is just being colonised: there, immigration may contribute more significantly to population growth than birth rates. So if a question asks when immigration matters more than natality, the answer is 'when a new habitat is being colonised'.

The board likes to ask this section as a flow chart: draw a box labelled 'population density (N)', two arrows entering it labelled natality and immigration, two arrows leaving it labelled mortality and emigration, and write the equation beneath. That figure plus the four definitions is a complete 3-mark answer.

where: natality, number of births in the period
immigration, individuals of the same species that entered the habitat
emigration, individuals that left the habitat

sections.tip: Natality, mortality, immigration and emigration are numbers of individuals over a period. Birth rate and death rate are those numbers divided by the population size. Do not mix the two when a question gives raw counts.

sections.heading: 11.1.2 Population Growth (continued): exponential and logistic growth models
sections.body:
This is the most examined part of the chapter, and it appears as a 5-mark question, a 3-mark 'draw and compare' and a 4-mark case with a graph. Learn both models with their equations, curves and conditions.

Exponential (geometric) growth. Resource (food and space) availability is essential for unimpeded growth. When resources in the habitat are unlimited, each species can realise fully its innate potential to grow in number, as Darwin observed while developing his theory of natural selection, and the population grows in an exponential or geometric fashion. If a population of size N has a per-capita birth rate b and a per-capita death rate d, the change in N during a unit time period t is dN/dt = (b − d) × N. Writing (b − d) = r, this becomes dN/dt = rN. The r is called the intrinsic rate of natural increase, and NCERT calls it a very important parameter for assessing the impact of any biotic or abiotic factor on population growth. The values to remember: the r for the Norway rat is 0.015, for the flour beetle 0.12, and for the human population in India in 1981 it was 0.0205. Plotting N against time gives a J-shaped curve. The integral form of the equation is Nt = N0 ert, where Nt is the population density after time t, N0 the density at time zero, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase and e the base of natural logarithms (2.71828). Any species growing exponentially under unlimited resources can reach enormous densities in a short time; Darwin showed how even a slow-growing animal like the elephant could reach enormous numbers in the absence of checks. The NCERT exercise uses the integral form: if a population doubles in 3 years, 2 = e3r, so r = ln 2/3 = 0.693/3 ≈ 0.231 per year.

Logistic growth. No population in nature has unlimited resources, so exponential growth cannot continue. Limited resources lead to competition between individuals, and eventually the 'fittest' individuals survive and reproduce. A given habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible; this limit is called nature's carrying capacity (K) for that species in that habitat. A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows initially a lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when the density reaches the carrying capacity. Plotting N against t gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. This is Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth, described by dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), where N is the population density at time t, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K the carrying capacity. Notice what the bracket does: when N is small, (K − N)/K is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential; as N approaches K the bracket approaches 0 and growth stops.

Which is realistic? NCERT's sentence, which should be quoted: since resources for growth for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered a more realistic one. On the NCERT graph, curve (a) is exponential growth when resources are not limiting and curve (b) is logistic growth when resources are limiting, with K drawn as a horizontal dotted line that the logistic curve approaches.

where: intrinsic rate of natural increase, r = b − d
carrying capacity of the habitat for that species
the unused fraction of the carrying capacity; it falls to zero as N reaches K

sections.tip: In the 5-mark answer, write the assumptions (resources unlimited versus limited), the differential equation, the name of the curve, the labelled curve and the meaning of every symbol. For the logistic model add the four phases and the sentence on why it is more realistic. Each of those is a marking point.

sections.heading: 11.1.3 Life History Variation
sections.body:
This short section carries a definition that has appeared as a 3-mark question: Darwinian fitness. Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness, which NCERT equates with a high r value, in the habitat in which they live. Under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy. The strategies differ in two ways, and each has NCERT examples that are asked by name.

  • How often they breed. Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime: the Pacific salmon fish and bamboo. Others breed many times during their lifetime: most birds and mammals. Bamboo flowering is a classic 1-mark question ('mention the unique feature of flowering and fruiting in bamboo'): it flowers once in its life, often after decades, and then dies.
  • How many offspring and how large. Some produce a large number of small-sized offspring: oysters and pelagic fishes. Others produce a small number of large-sized offspring: birds and mammals.

NCERT then asks which strategy is desirable for maximising fitness and answers that there is no single answer: ecologists suggest that life history traits of organisms have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat in which they live. That sentence is the reason a question on this section is usually worded 'why do different organisms have different reproductive strategies'.

An Assertion–Reason on this section usually pairs 'organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy' with 'the strategy is decided by the selection pressures of the habitat'; both are true and the reason explains the assertion.
sections.tip: Darwinian fitness in this chapter means reproductive fitness measured as a high r value. Do not describe it as physical strength or 'survival of the strongest'.

sections.heading: 11.1.4 Population Interactions: the six types and the +/−/0 table
sections.body:
NCERT begins with a question: can you think of any natural habitat on earth inhabited by just a single species? There is none. Animals, plants and microbes do not and cannot live in isolation; they interact in various ways to form a biological community. For any species the minimal requirement is one more species on which it can feed. Even a plant, which makes its own food, cannot survive alone: it needs soil microbes to break down organic matter and return inorganic nutrients for absorption, and it needs an animal agent for pollination. So a community with at least two species is the minimum.

Interspecific interactions arise from the interaction of populations of two different species. They may be beneficial, detrimental or neutral (neither harmful nor beneficial) to one of the species or to both. Assigning + for a beneficial effect, − for a detrimental effect and 0 for a neutral one, the six possible outcomes are the table the board keeps asking for:

  • Mutualism: + / +. Both species benefit.
  • Competition: − / −. Both species lose.
  • Predation: + / −. The predator benefits, the prey is harmed.
  • Parasitism: + / −. The parasite benefits, the host is harmed.
  • Commensalism: + / 0. One species benefits, the other is neither benefited nor harmed.
  • Amensalism: − / 0. One species is harmed, the other is unaffected.

NCERT adds one connecting sentence that examiners like: predation, parasitism and commensalism share a common characteristic, that the interacting species live closely together. A typical 2-mark question gives six pairs of organisms and asks you to name the interaction for each; a 3-mark version gives a table with letters A to D in place of the signs or the names and asks you to fill them in. The rest of the chapter takes the interactions one at a time, in NCERT order: predation, competition, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism. Amensalism has no separate section in NCERT; if you need an example, the inhibition of bacteria by the antibiotic secreted by Penicillium is the standard one.
sections.tip: In the table, write the sign of species A and species B in the same order for every row (A first, then B). Predation and parasitism both read + / −, so add 'predator/prey' and 'parasite/host' to show you know which is which.

sections.heading: Predation: roles of predators and the defences of prey
sections.body:
NCERT starts with a point that has been asked as a 2-mark question: although animals eating plants are categorised separately as herbivores, in a broad ecological context they are not very different from predators. For a plant, the herbivore is the predator.

Roles of predators. The obvious role is that predators act as 'conduits' for energy transfer across trophic levels: the energy fixed by plants moves up the food chain through them. NCERT lists three further roles, and 'mention two roles of predators other than energy transfer' is a regular question.

  1. They keep prey populations under control. Without predators, prey species could reach very high densities and cause ecosystem instability. When an exotic species is introduced into a new area it becomes invasive and spreads fast because the invaded land has no natural predators of it. The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s spread into millions of hectares of rangeland and was brought under control only when a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced. This is the ecological principle behind biological control of agricultural pests: the ability of a predator to regulate its prey population (NCERT exercise question 5).
  2. They help maintain species diversity in a community by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species. In the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast the starfish Pisaster is an important predator; when all the starfish were removed from an enclosed intertidal area in a field experiment, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year because of interspecific competition.
  3. Predators are 'prudent'. If a predator is too efficient and overexploits its prey, the prey may become extinct and the predator will follow for lack of food. That is why predators in nature are prudent.

Defences of prey animals. Some species of insects and frogs are cryptically coloured (camouflaged) to avoid detection. Some are poisonous and are avoided. The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator (a bird) because of a special chemical in its body, which the butterfly acquires during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed. The source of the chemical is the detail the examiner checks.

Defences of plants. Nearly 25 per cent of all insects are phytophagous (they feed on plant sap and other plant parts). Plants cannot run away, so they have evolved morphological and chemical defences. Thorns (Acacia, Cactus) are the commonest morphological defence. Many plants make and store chemicals that make the herbivore sick, inhibit its feeding or digestion, disrupt its reproduction or kill it. The weed Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, which is why cattle and goats never browse on it. The substances we extract from plants commercially, nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium, are produced by plants as defences against grazers and browsers.
sections.tip: For 'why do cattle and goats not browse on Calotropis', name the chemical: cardiac glycosides. 'Because it is poisonous' alone is half the mark.

sections.heading: Competition: Gause's principle, competitive release and resource partitioning
sections.body:
When Darwin spoke of the struggle for existence and survival of the fittest, he was convinced that interspecific competition is a potent force in organic evolution. It is generally believed that competition occurs when closely related species compete for the same limiting resources, but NCERT makes two corrections. First, totally unrelated species can compete: in some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton. Second, resources need not be limiting: in interference competition the feeding efficiency of one species is reduced by the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other, even when food and space are abundant. So NCERT defines competition as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured as its r) is significantly lower in the presence of another species.

In the laboratory, as Gause and others showed, when resources are limited the competitively superior species eventually eliminates the other. Evidence for such competitive exclusion in nature is not always conclusive, but there are circumstantial evidences. (1) The Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, apparently because of the greater browsing efficiency of the goats. (2) Competitive release: a species restricted to a small area by a competitively superior species expands its range dramatically when the competitor is experimentally removed. Connell's field experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland showed that the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chathamalus from that zone. In general, herbivores and plants are more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.

Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. NCERT qualifies it at once: this may be true if resources are limiting, but not otherwise. More recent studies do not support such gross generalisations. They do not rule out interspecific competition in nature, but point out that species facing competition may evolve mechanisms that promote coexistence rather than exclusion. One such mechanism is resource partitioning: two species that compete for the same resource avoid competition by choosing, for instance, different times for feeding or different foraging patterns. MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree coexist because of behavioural differences in their foraging activities. The 2-mark question 'state Gause's principle and how recent studies have modified it' wants the principle, the qualification, and resource partitioning with the warbler example.
sections.tip: Balanus is the larger, competitively superior barnacle; Chathamalus is the smaller one that gets excluded. Students swap them. Write 'Connell, rocky sea coasts of Scotland' with the names.

sections.heading: Parasitism: adaptations, life cycles, ectoparasites, endoparasites and brood parasitism
sections.body:
The parasitic mode of life ensures free lodging and meals, so it is not surprising that parasitism has evolved in so many groups, from plants to higher vertebrates. Many parasites are host-specific (they can parasitise only a single host species), and host and parasite tend to co-evolve: if the host evolves special mechanisms for rejecting or resisting the parasite, the parasite has to evolve mechanisms to counteract and neutralise them to remain successful with the same host. This is the standard answer to 'explain co-evolution with reference to parasites'.

Adaptations of parasites, four of them, asked almost every year: (1) loss of unnecessary sense organs, (2) presence of adhesive organs or suckers to cling on to the host, (3) loss of the digestive system, and (4) high reproductive capacity.

Life cycles. Parasite life cycles are often complex, involving one or two intermediate hosts or vectors to facilitate parasitisation of the primary host. The human liver fluke (a trematode) depends on two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish, to complete its life cycle. The malarial parasite needs a vector (mosquito) to spread to other hosts.

Harm to the host. Most parasites reduce the survival, growth and reproduction of the host and reduce its population density, and they may make the host physically weak and so more vulnerable to predation. NCERT asks why natural selection did not produce a totally harmless parasite that thrives without harming its host; the expected reasoning is that a parasite necessarily takes nutrients from the host, so some harm is unavoidable.

Ectoparasites feed on the external surface of the host: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, and the copepods that infest many marine fish. Cuscuta, a parasitic plant found growing on hedge plants, has lost its chlorophyll and leaves in the course of evolution and draws its nutrition from the host. The female mosquito is not considered a parasite, although it needs our blood for reproduction: it does not live on or in the host, it only takes a brief blood meal and leaves. Endoparasites live inside the host body at sites such as the liver, kidney, lungs and red blood cells. Their life cycles are more complex because of their extreme specialisation, and their morphological and anatomical features are greatly simplified while their reproductive potential is emphasised.

Brood parasitism in birds: the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them. Over evolution the eggs of the parasitic bird have come to resemble the host's eggs in size and colour, which reduces the chance of the host detecting the foreign eggs and ejecting them. The NCERT example is the cuckoo (koel) and the crow, which you can watch in a park during the breeding season, spring to summer.
sections.tip: For brood parasitism give both halves: what the cuckoo does (lays eggs in the crow's nest, crow incubates them) and the adaptation (eggs resemble the crow's in size and colour). The adaptation carries its own mark.

sections.heading: Commensalism
sections.body:
Commensalism is the interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited, the + / 0 row of the table. NCERT gives four examples and each has been asked on its own as a 1- or 2-mark question, so learn all four with the reason the second species is unaffected.

  • An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch. The orchid gets a place to grow and access to light; the mango tree derives no apparent benefit and is not harmed, because the orchid does not draw nutrients from it. This is NCERT exercise question 4 and appeared as a 1-mark board question ('an orchid growing on a forest tree: name the interaction').
  • Barnacles growing on the back of a whale. The barnacles get a substrate and are carried through plankton-rich water; the whale is unaffected.
  • Cattle egret and grazing cattle, a sight common in farmed rural areas. The egrets forage close to the cattle because the cattle, as they move, stir up and flush out insects from the vegetation that the egrets would otherwise find hard to catch. The cattle gain nothing and lose nothing.
  • Clown fish and sea anemone. The sea anemone has stinging tentacles and the clown fish lives among them; the fish gets protection from predators, which stay away from the stinging tentacles. The anemone does not appear to derive any benefit from hosting the fish.

Two comparisons are asked. Commensalism versus mutualism: in mutualism both benefit (lichen, mycorrhiza), in commensalism only one does (epiphytic orchid, egret). Commensalism versus parasitism: in both, the interacting species live closely together, but in parasitism the second species is harmed (Cuscuta on a hedge plant) whereas in commensalism it is unaffected (orchid on a mango branch). When a question asks you to 'differentiate with plant examples', use the orchid for commensalism, Cuscuta for parasitism and mycorrhiza or lichen for mutualism.

One trap: students sometimes call the clown fish and sea anemone relationship mutualism because popular sources say the fish cleans the anemone or lures prey to it. The NCERT position, and therefore the marking scheme's, is commensalism: the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit. Write what NCERT says.
sections.tip: For any commensalism example, write one line on what the benefiting species gains and one line saying the other species is neither harmed nor benefited. The second line is where the second mark sits.

sections.heading: Mutualism: lichens, mycorrhizae, fig and wasp, Ophrys and the bee
sections.body:
Mutualism confers benefits on both interacting species. Lichens are an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria. Mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and the roots of higher plants: the fungi help the plant absorb essential nutrients from the soil, and the plant in turn provides the fungi with energy-yielding carbohydrates. These two are the 'commercially exploited' or 'plant' examples of mutualism that 2-mark questions ask for.

Plant-animal mutualisms. The most spectacular examples are plant-animal relationships. Plants need animals for pollination and seed dispersal, and animals have to be paid 'fees' for these services. Plants offer rewards: pollen and nectar for pollinators, and juicy, nutritious fruits for seed dispersers. The system also has to be safeguarded against 'cheaters', for example animals that steal nectar without pollinating. This is why plant-animal interactions often involve co-evolution of the mutualists: the evolution of the flower and of its pollinator species are tightly linked.

Fig and wasp. In many species of fig trees there is a tight one-to-one relationship with the pollinator species of wasp: a given fig species can be pollinated only by its 'partner' wasp species and by no other. The female wasp uses the fruit as an oviposition (egg-laying) site and uses the developing seeds within the fruit to nourish its larvae. The wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites. In return for pollination, the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds as food for the wasp larvae. This has been a 2- or 3-mark question in each of the last two board papers; write the four points above in order.

Orchids and Ophrys. Orchids show a bewildering diversity of floral patterns, many evolved to attract the right pollinator insect (bees and bumblebees) and ensure guaranteed pollination. Not all orchids offer rewards. The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs 'sexual deceit' to get pollinated by a species of bee: one petal of its flower bears an uncanny resemblance to the female of the bee in size, colour and markings. The male bee is attracted to what it perceives as a female, 'pseudocopulates' with the flower and in the process is dusted with pollen. When the same bee pseudocopulates with another flower it transfers the pollen and so pollinates it. NCERT uses this to show how co-evolution operates: if the female bee's colour patterns change even slightly during evolution, pollination success will fall unless the orchid flower co-evolves to maintain the resemblance of its petal to the female bee. A 3-mark question asks what would happen to the orchid if the bee went extinct: the orchid would fail to be pollinated and would itself decline, because it depends on that one pollinator.
sections.tip: In the Ophrys answer use NCERT's own words: 'sexual deceit', 'pseudocopulates', 'one petal resembles the female bee in size, colour and markings', and finish with the co-evolution sentence. Marking schemes are keyed to these phrases.

key_terms.definition: The study of the interactions among organisms and between the organism and its physical (abiotic) environment; it works at four levels: organisms, populations, communities and biomes.

A group of individuals of the same species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources and potentially interbreeding, e.g. lotus plants in a pond or rats in an abandoned dwelling.
An assemblage of populations of different species living together and interacting in a given area; the minimum community has two species, since every species needs at least one other to feed on.
The number of births per individual per unit time in a population; 8 new lotus plants added to 20 gives 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.
The number of deaths per individual per unit time; 4 deaths in 40 fruit flies in a week gives 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.
The proportion of males and females in a population, e.g. 60 per cent females and 40 per cent males; an attribute a population has and an individual does not.

A plot of the age distribution (per cent individuals in each age group: pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive) of a population; its shape shows whether the population is expanding, stable or declining.

The size of a population, expressed as the total number of individuals, or where more meaningful as biomass or per cent cover, or estimated as a relative density (fish per trap) or indirectly (tiger pug marks and fecal pellets).
The number of births during a given period in the population that are added to the initial density.
The number of deaths in the population during a given period.

The number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during the period under consideration; it adds to density and matters most when a new habitat is being colonised.
The number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and went elsewhere during the period; it reduces density.
The difference between per-capita birth rate and per-capita death rate, r = b − d; the growth parameter of both models. Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, India in 1981 0.0205.
Growth under unlimited resources described by dN/dt = rN and N<sub>t</sub> = N<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup>, giving a J-shaped curve.
The maximum number of individuals of a species that a habitat can support with its resources, beyond which no further growth is possible; the asymptote of the logistic curve.
Growth under limited resources described by dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), showing lag, acceleration, deceleration and asymptote phases in a sigmoid curve; considered the more realistic model.
Reproductive fitness, a high r value, which populations evolve to maximise in the habitat where they live.

An interaction between populations of two different species that may be beneficial (+), detrimental (−) or neutral (0) to each; the six outcomes are mutualism, competition, predation, parasitism, commensalism and amensalism.

A + / − interaction in which one species (predator) kills and eats another (prey); herbivory is predation in the ecological sense. Predators transfer energy across trophic levels, control prey numbers and maintain species diversity.
Managing pests by introducing their natural predators; based on the ability of the predator to regulate the prey population, e.g. the moth introduced against prickly pear cactus in Australia.
Colouring that lets a prey species, such as some insects and frogs, avoid detection by predators.

A − / − interaction in which the fitness (r) of one species is significantly lower in the presence of another; it can occur between unrelated species (flamingoes and fishes) and even when resources are not limiting (interference competition).
Two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually; true only when resources are limiting.
The dramatic expansion of a species' range when a competitively superior species is removed, shown by Connell's Balanus and Chathamalus barnacles on the Scottish coast.
A mechanism promoting coexistence in which competing species use the resource at different times or with different foraging patterns; MacArthur's five warbler species on one tree.

A + / − interaction in which the parasite lives on or in a host and draws nutrition from it, harming the host; parasites show loss of sense organs and digestive system, suckers and high reproductive capacity.

An ectoparasite feeds on the external surface of the host (lice, ticks, copepods on marine fish, Cuscuta on hedge plants); an endoparasite lives inside the host body (liver, kidney, lungs, red blood cells).
A parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of a host bird, which incubates them; the cuckoo's eggs resemble the crow's in size and colour so they are not detected and ejected.

A + / 0 interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited: an epiphytic orchid on a mango branch, barnacles on a whale, cattle egret and cattle, clown fish and sea anemone.
A + / + interaction benefiting both species: lichens (fungus and alga or cyanobacterium), mycorrhizae (fungus and plant roots), fig and its wasp, plants and their pollinators.
Linked evolution of two interacting species, such as a host and its parasite, or the orchid Ophrys and the bee whose female its petal resembles.
The pollination strategy of the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys, whose petal mimics a female bee so that the male bee pseudocopulates with the flower and is dusted with pollen.

formula_sheet.name: Population equation
formula_sheet.note: B natality, I immigration add; D mortality, E emigration remove. Births and deaths matter most normally; immigration matters more when a new habitat is being colonised.

formula_sheet.name: Exponential growth
formula_sheet.expr: dN/dt = (b − d) × N = rN; integral form N<sub>t</sub> = N<sub>0</sub> e<sup>rt</sup>, e = 2.71828
formula_sheet.note: Resources unlimited; J-shaped curve; doubling in 3 years gives r = ln 2/3 ≈ 0.231 per year

formula_sheet.name: Logistic (Verhulst-Pearl) growth
formula_sheet.note: Resources limited; sigmoid curve with lag, acceleration, deceleration, asymptote at K; the more realistic model

formula_sheet.name: Values of r
formula_sheet.expr: Norway rat 0.015 · flour beetle 0.12 · human population of India (1981) 0.0205
formula_sheet.note: r = intrinsic rate of natural increase = per-capita birth rate minus per-capita death rate

formula_sheet.name: Birth-rate and death-rate examples
formula_sheet.expr: Lotus: 8 new plants in a pond of 20 → 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year · Fruit flies: 4 deaths in 40 in a week → 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week
formula_sheet.note: Divide by the initial population; state the unit

formula_sheet.name: Population attributes an individual lacks
formula_sheet.expr: Birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age distribution (age pyramid), population size or density
formula_sheet.note: NCERT exercise 1 and 10; explain each in one line

formula_sheet.name: Age pyramids
formula_sheet.expr: Expanding (growing): broad base, triangular · Stable: bell-shaped, pre-reproductive ≈ reproductive · Declining: narrow base, urn-shaped
formula_sheet.note: Age groups: pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive; used for planning human populations

formula_sheet.name: Measuring density
formula_sheet.expr: Number of individuals · biomass or per cent cover (single huge banyan vs 200 Parthenium) · relative density (fish per trap) · indirect estimation (tiger census by pug marks and fecal pellets)
formula_sheet.note: Range in nature: under 10 (Siberian cranes at Bharatpur) to millions (Chlamydomonas in a pond)

formula_sheet.name: Interaction table
formula_sheet.expr: Mutualism + / + · Competition − / − · Predation + / − · Parasitism + / − · Commensalism + / 0 · Amensalism − / 0
formula_sheet.note: Predation, parasitism and commensalism: the interacting species live closely together

formula_sheet.name: Life history variation
formula_sheet.expr: Breed once: Pacific salmon, bamboo · Breed many times: most birds and mammals · Many small offspring: oysters, pelagic fishes · Few large offspring: birds, mammals
formula_sheet.note: Traits evolved under the constraints of the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat; Darwinian fitness = high r

formula_sheet.name: Predation examples
formula_sheet.expr: Prickly pear cactus in Australia (1920s) controlled by a cactus-feeding moth · Pisaster starfish removal on the American Pacific Coast → over 10 invertebrate species extinct within a year · Monarch butterfly toxin from a poisonous weed eaten as a caterpillar · thorns of Acacia and Cactus · cardiac glycosides of Calotropis · nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium
formula_sheet.note: Nearly 25 per cent of all insects are phytophagous; predators are 'prudent'

formula_sheet.name: Competition examples
formula_sheet.expr: Flamingoes and resident fishes (zooplankton, South American lakes) · Abingdon tortoise extinct within a decade of goats reaching Galapagos · Connell: Balanus (larger, superior) excludes Chathamalus (smaller) on Scottish rocky coasts, competitive release · MacArthur: five warbler species on one tree, resource partitioning
formula_sheet.note: Herbivores and plants suffer more from competition than carnivores

formula_sheet.name: Parasitism facts
formula_sheet.expr: Adaptations: loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs or suckers, loss of digestive system, high reproductive capacity · Human liver fluke: two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish · Malarial parasite: vector mosquito · Ectoparasites: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on marine fish, Cuscuta on hedges (no chlorophyll, no leaves) · Endoparasites: liver, kidney, lungs, RBCs · Brood parasitism: cuckoo (koel) in crow's nest
formula_sheet.note: The female mosquito is not a parasite

formula_sheet.name: Commensalism and mutualism examples
formula_sheet.expr: Commensalism: orchid on mango branch, barnacles on whale, cattle egret and cattle, clown fish and sea anemone · Mutualism: lichen (fungus + alga/cyanobacterium), mycorrhiza (fungus + plant roots), fig and its one partner wasp, Ophrys and the male bee (sexual deceit, pseudocopulation)
formula_sheet.note: Rewards: pollen and nectar for pollinators, fruits for dispersers; guard against 'cheaters'

diagrams.title: The three age pyramids (NCERT Fig. 11.1 style)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three outlines side by side, each with a vertical axis marked in three bands from bottom to top: pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive, and a central vertical line dividing males (left) from females (right). Pyramid (a) is a broad-based triangle labelled 'expanding (growing)'; pyramid (b) is bell-shaped with the pre-reproductive and reproductive bands nearly equal in width, labelled 'stable'; pyramid (c) is urn-shaped with a narrow base and a wider middle and top, labelled 'declining'. The three shapes, the three age-group labels and the growth status under each earn full marks.

diagrams.title: Population growth curves: exponential (a) and logistic (b) (NCERT Fig. 11.2 style)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Axes: population density (N) upward, time (t) rightward. Draw a horizontal dotted line high on the graph labelled 'K, carrying capacity'. From a low starting point on the left draw curve (a) rising ever more steeply and crossing the K line, labelled 'exponential growth, dN/dt = rN, resources not limiting'. From the same start draw curve (b) rising slowly, then steeply, then flattening to run just under the dotted K line, labelled 'logistic growth, dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), resources limiting'. Label the two curves (a) and (b) and write both equations on the figure.

diagrams.title: The logistic (sigmoid) curve with its four phases
diagrams.how_to_draw: Same axes as above with the dotted K line. Draw a single S-shaped curve and bracket four regions along it: the nearly flat start labelled 'lag phase', the steepening middle labelled 'acceleration phase' (mark the point of steepest slope, near K/2), the flattening upper part labelled 'deceleration phase', and the final flat run under the K line labelled 'asymptote (N = K)'. Write the equation and 'Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth' as the title.

diagrams.title: Flow chart of the four processes that change population density
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a central box labelled 'Population density (N)'. Two arrows enter it from the left, labelled 'natality (B)' and 'immigration (I)', with a '+' sign. Two arrows leave it to the right, labelled 'mortality (D)' and 'emigration (E)', with a '−' sign. Under the box write N<sub>t+1</sub> = N<sub>t</sub> + [(B + I) − (D + E)] and the sentence 'density increases when (B + I) > (D + E)'. Examiners award marks for the four labelled arrows and the equation.

diagrams.title: The interspecific interaction table (NCERT Table 11.1 style)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a table with three columns headed 'Species A', 'Species B', 'Name of interaction' and six rows: + + mutualism; − − competition; + − predation; + − parasitism; + 0 commensalism; − 0 amensalism. Add a fourth column with one NCERT example per row (lichen; Balanus and Chathamalus; Pisaster and intertidal invertebrates; Cuscuta on hedge; orchid on mango; Penicillium and bacteria). Boards give this table with blanks and ask you to complete it, so practise reproducing it from memory.

diagrams.title: Connell's barnacle experiment: competitive release on a rocky shore
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a sloping rocky shore in section with the sea on the right; mark a horizontal line for high tide and one for low tide, and label the band between them 'intertidal zone'. In the natural state (left panel) draw the larger barnacle Balanus filling the lower intertidal band and the smaller Chathamalus confined to a thin band above it; label them and write 'Balanus, larger and competitively superior, excludes Chathamalus'. In the right panel show Balanus removed and Chathamalus spread down through the whole intertidal band; label 'competitive release'. Title it 'Connell, rocky sea coasts of Scotland'.

diagrams.title: Sexual deceit in the orchid Ophrys
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an orchid flower with a large lower petal (the lip) shaded and marked with bands to look like the body of a female bee, and label it 'one petal resembles the female bee in size, colour and markings'. Above it draw a male bee landing on the petal, label 'male bee pseudocopulates with the flower' and mark the pollen mass touching the bee's head or back, labelled 'pollen dusted onto the bee'. Add an arrow to a second Ophrys flower labelled 'pollen transferred, flower pollinated'. Under the figure write 'co-evolution: if the female bee's pattern changes, the orchid must change to keep the resemblance'.

diagrams.title: Mycorrhiza and lichen: two mutualisms in one sketch
diagrams.how_to_draw: Left half: draw a plant root with a mesh of fungal hyphae wrapped around and extending into the soil; label 'root of higher plant', 'fungal hyphae', and two arrows: from fungus to root labelled 'essential nutrients (phosphorus, water) absorbed from soil', from root to fungus labelled 'energy-yielding carbohydrates'. Right half: draw a crust of lichen in section with fungal hyphae enclosing a layer of round green algal (or cyanobacterial) cells; label 'fungal hyphae (absorbs water, minerals, gives protection)' and 'algal or cyanobacterial cells (photosynthesis, food)'. Write '+ / + mutualism' under both.

diagrams.title: Defences of plants against herbivores
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two plant sketches. First an Acacia or cactus stem bearing prominent thorns, labelled 'morphological defence: thorns (Acacia, Cactus)'. Second a Calotropis shoot with its broad leaves and a drop of latex, labelled 'chemical defence: cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats do not browse'. Beside them list the commercially extracted defensive chemicals: nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium. Add the line 'nearly 25 per cent of all insects are phytophagous' as the reason plants need defences.

ncert_questions.q: List the attributes that populations possess but not individuals.
ncert_questions.a:
A population has attributes that an individual organism does not:

  1. Birth rate (natality): an individual is born once, but a population has a birth rate, the number of births per individual per unit time. Example: 8 new lotus plants in a pond of 20 give a birth rate of 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.
  2. Death rate (mortality): an individual dies once, but a population has a death rate. Example: 4 deaths in a week among 40 fruit flies give 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.
  3. Sex ratio: an individual is male or female; a population has a sex ratio, e.g. 60 per cent females and 40 per cent males.
  4. Age distribution (age pyramid): a population contains individuals of different ages, and the per cent in each age group plotted as an age pyramid shows whether the population is expanding, stable or declining.
  5. Population size or density (N): the total number or biomass of individuals in the population.

ncert_questions.q: If a population growing exponentially doubles in size in 3 years, what is the intrinsic rate of increase (r) of the population?
ncert_questions.a:
Exponential growth in integral form: Nt = N0 ert.

The population doubles in 3 years, so Nt = 2N0 when t = 3.

2N0 = N0 e3r → 2 = e3r

Taking natural logarithms: ln 2 = 3r → r = ln 2 / 3 = 0.693 / 3 = 0.231 per year.

Check: e0.231 × 3 = e0.693 ≈ 2. The intrinsic rate of natural increase is about 0.231 (23.1 per cent per year).

ncert_questions.q: Name important defence mechanisms in plants against herbivory.
ncert_questions.a:
Plants cannot run away from herbivores, so they have evolved morphological and chemical defences.

  • Morphological defences: thorns are the most common, as in Acacia and Cactus. Spines, prickles and tough leaves also deter feeding.
  • Chemical defences: many plants produce and store chemicals that make the herbivore sick when eaten, inhibit its feeding or digestion, disrupt its reproduction or kill it. Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, which is why cattle and goats never browse on it. Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium, which we extract commercially, are produced by plants as defences against grazers and browsers.

ncert_questions.q: An orchid plant is growing on the branch of a mango tree. How do you describe this interaction between the orchid and the mango tree?
ncert_questions.a: The interaction is commensalism. The orchid grows as an epiphyte on the mango branch and benefits by getting a place to grow and better access to sunlight. The mango tree is neither harmed nor benefited: the orchid does not draw water or nutrients from the mango, it only uses the branch as a support. In the interaction table this is the + / 0 relationship, with the orchid as + and the mango as 0.

ncert_questions.q: What is the ecological principle behind the biological control method of managing pest insects?
ncert_questions.a: The principle is predation: the ability of a predator to regulate the population of its prey. Predators keep prey populations under control; without them prey could reach very high densities and destabilise the ecosystem. In biological control a natural predator or parasite of the pest is introduced so that it keeps the pest population below damaging levels without chemical pesticides. NCERT's example is the prickly pear cactus, which spread over millions of hectares of rangeland in Australia after its introduction in the early 1920s and was brought under control only when a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced.

Population: a group of individuals of the same species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources and potentially interbreeding. Examples: cormorants in a wetland, rats in an abandoned dwelling, teakwood trees in a forest tract, bacteria in a culture plate, lotus plants in a pond.

Community: an assemblage of populations of different species living together and interacting with one another in a given area. Even the smallest community has at least two species, because every species needs at least one other species to feed on; even a plant needs soil microbes to recycle nutrients and an animal agent for pollination.

ncert_questions.q: Define the following terms and give one example for each: (a) Commensalism (b) Parasitism (c) Camouflage (d) Mutualism (e) Interspecific competition.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Commensalism: an interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited (+ / 0). Example: an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch; the cattle egret feeding on insects flushed out by grazing cattle.

(b) Parasitism: an interaction in which one species (the parasite) lives on or in another (the host), drawing nutrition from it and harming it (+ / −). Example: Cuscuta on hedge plants; ticks on dogs; the human liver fluke.

(c) Camouflage: cryptic colouration or pattern by which a prey organism blends with its surroundings and avoids detection by predators. Example: cryptically coloured insects and frogs.

(d) Mutualism: an interaction in which both species benefit (+ / +). Example: lichens (fungus and alga or cyanobacterium); mycorrhizae (fungus and plant roots); fig and its pollinator wasp.

(e) Interspecific competition: an interaction between two different species in which the fitness (r) of one species is significantly lower in the presence of the other, usually because they use the same resource (− / −). Example: flamingoes and resident fishes competing for zooplankton in South American lakes; the Abingdon tortoise driven extinct by goats in the Galapagos.

ncert_questions.q: With the help of a suitable diagram describe the logistic population growth curve.
ncert_questions.a:
No population in nature has unlimited resources. A habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number of a species, beyond which no further growth is possible; this limit is the carrying capacity (K). A population growing with limited resources shows initially a lag phase, then phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when the density reaches K. A plot of N against time gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. This is Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth, described by

dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K)

where N = population density at time t, r = intrinsic rate of natural increase, K = carrying capacity. When N is small the factor (K − N)/K is nearly 1 and growth is almost exponential; as N approaches K the factor approaches 0 and growth stops.

Diagram: axes N (vertical) and t (horizontal); a horizontal dotted line labelled K; an S-shaped curve starting low, rising slowly (lag), then steeply (acceleration), then flattening (deceleration) to run just under the K line (asymptote). Label all four phases, the K line and the equation.

Since resources for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic model is considered more realistic than the exponential model.

ncert_questions.q: Select the statement which explains best parasitism: (a) One organism is benefited. (b) Both organisms are benefited. (c) One organism is benefited, other is not affected. (d) One organism is benefited, and another is affected.
ncert_questions.a: (d) One organism is benefited, and another is affected. In parasitism the parasite benefits and the host is harmed (+ / −). Option (b) describes mutualism and option (c) commensalism; option (a) is incomplete because it does not say what happens to the second organism.

ncert_questions.q: List any three important characteristics of a population and explain.
ncert_questions.a:
1. Population density (size, N): the total number of individuals of the species in the given area at a given time, or where more meaningful the biomass or per cent cover (a single huge banyan tree versus 200 Parthenium plants). It can be measured as a relative density (fish caught per trap) or estimated indirectly (tiger census from pug marks and fecal pellets).

2. Birth rate and death rate: per-capita rates of addition and loss. Eight new lotus plants in a pond of 20 give a birth rate of 0.4 per lotus per year; 4 deaths among 40 fruit flies in a week give a death rate of 0.1 per fruit fly per week. Together with immigration and emigration they decide whether the population grows or shrinks.

3. Age distribution: the proportion of individuals in the pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive age groups, plotted as an age pyramid whose shape shows whether the population is expanding (broad base), stable (bell-shaped) or declining (urn-shaped).

(Sex ratio, the proportion of males and females, is a fourth characteristic.)

ncert_questions.q: In a pond there were 20 lotus plants last year and through reproduction 8 new plants were added, taking the population to 28. Calculate the birth rate.
ncert_questions.a: Birth rate = number of births ÷ initial population = 8 ÷ 20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year. The denominator is the initial population (20), not the current population (28).

ncert_questions.q: In a laboratory population of 40 fruit flies, 4 individuals died in a week. Calculate the death rate.
ncert_questions.a: Death rate = number of deaths ÷ population = 4 ÷ 40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week.

ncert_questions.q: The female mosquito is not considered a parasite, although it needs our blood for reproduction. Explain why.
ncert_questions.a: A parasite lives on or in its host for a prolonged period, drawing nutrition from it continuously and usually showing adaptations such as attachment organs. The female mosquito only takes a brief blood meal and leaves; it does not live on the host, does not depend on a single host and completes its life cycle away from the host. It is therefore treated as a micro-predator or a blood feeder, not as a parasite.

ncert_questions.q: Do you believe that an ideal parasite should be able to thrive within the host without harming it? Why didn't natural selection lead to the evolution of such totally harmless parasites?
ncert_questions.a: A completely harmless parasite is not possible because the parasite must draw nutrients from the host and use the host's body for its own growth and reproduction; whatever it takes is a loss to the host. Natural selection favours parasites that maximise their own reproduction (high reproductive capacity), and that necessarily reduces the host's survival, growth or reproduction. What selection does favour is a parasite that does not kill its host too quickly, since a dead host ends the parasite's own supply of food and lodging.

ncert_questions.q: What did Darwin show about the elephant, and what does it illustrate?
ncert_questions.a: Darwin showed that even a slow-growing animal like the elephant could reach enormous numbers in the absence of checks. It illustrates that any species growing exponentially under unlimited resources can reach enormous population densities in a short time, and hence that checks such as limited resources, predation and disease must be operating in nature, which is the basis of the logistic model and of the struggle for existence in natural selection.

pyq.q: A biologist studied the population of rats in a granary. He found that natality was 280, mortality 200, immigration 40 and emigration 50. The net increase in the population is:
pyq.answer: b

pyq.q: The Verhulst-Pearl equation dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K) describes:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The equation with the carrying capacity K is the logistic growth model, which gives a sigmoid curve; exponential growth is dN/dt = rN.

pyq.q: An orchid growing on the branch of a forest tree is an example of:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The epiphytic orchid benefits (support and light) while the tree is neither harmed nor benefited, which is commensalism (+ / 0).

pyq.q: Which of the following is the correct pairing of an interaction with its NCERT example?
options: Mutualism: cattle egret and grazing cattle
Commensalism: Cuscuta on a hedge plant
Parasitism: clown fish and sea anemone
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Connell's barnacles Balanus and Chathamalus are the example of interspecific competition and competitive release. The egret-cattle and clown fish-anemone pairs are commensalism, and Cuscuta is a parasite.

pyq.q: The Abingdon tortoise of the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade of the introduction of goats. The reason was:
options: Interspecific competition, the goats having greater browsing efficiency
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT cites this as circumstantial evidence for competition in nature: the goats out-browsed the tortoise for the same vegetation.

pyq.q: The Monarch butterfly is distasteful to birds because of a chemical that it:
options: Synthesises in its wings as an adult
Acquires as a caterpillar by feeding on a poisonous weed
Obtains from the nectar of Calotropis as an adult
Produces from cardiac glycosides in its own glands
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT: the butterfly acquires the chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed.

pyq.q: The intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) of the human population of India in 1981 was:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: NCERT gives 0.0205 for India in 1981; 0.015 is the Norway rat and 0.12 the flour beetle.

pyq.q: In an age pyramid of a human population, a very broad base of pre-reproductive individuals indicates that the population is:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A triangular pyramid with a broad base means many young individuals about to enter the reproductive age, so the population is growing.

pyq.q: Which process contributes to a decrease in population density?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Emigration and mortality decrease density; natality and immigration increase it.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The logistic growth model is considered more realistic than the exponential growth model. Reason (R): Resources for growth for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: This is NCERT's own justification: because resources become limiting, growth cannot stay exponential and the logistic curve with a carrying capacity fits nature better.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Predators in nature are 'prudent'. Reason (R): If a predator is too efficient and overexploits its prey, the prey may become extinct and the predator will then also become extinct for lack of food.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT gives exactly this reasoning for why predators do not overexploit their prey.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The female Anopheles mosquito is a parasite of humans. Reason (R): It needs a blood meal from a human for reproduction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: NCERT states that the female mosquito is not considered a parasite although it needs our blood for reproduction; it takes a brief meal and leaves rather than living on the host. A is false, R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The eggs of the cuckoo resemble those of the crow in size and colour. Reason (R): The resemblance reduces the chance of the crow detecting the foreign eggs and ejecting them from its nest.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: This is the adaptation of brood parasitism described in NCERT; the resemblance evolved because it prevents detection and ejection.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): For a single huge banyan tree in a field of 200 Parthenium plants, per cent cover or biomass is a better measure of population size than number. Reason (R): Stating that the banyan's density is low relative to Parthenium underestimates its enormous role in the community.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT's example: counting alone misrepresents the banyan's importance, so biomass or per cent cover is the more meaningful measure.

pyq.q: Name two methods by which the population density of tigers in a national park can be estimated without counting them.
pyq.answer: The tiger census in national parks and tiger reserves is often based on indirect estimation, without actually counting or seeing the animals, using (i) pug marks (footprints, which are distinctive for individual tigers) and (ii) fecal pellets (scats) collected in the area. Either method gives an estimate of the number of individuals present.

pyq.q: State Gause's competitive exclusion principle. How have recent studies modified it?
pyq.answer:
Gause's principle: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually. This holds only when resources are limiting.

Modification: more recent studies do not support such a gross generalisation. Species facing competition may evolve mechanisms that promote coexistence rather than exclusion, such as resource partitioning, in which the species use the resource at different times or with different foraging patterns. MacArthur showed that five closely related warbler species on the same tree coexist because of behavioural differences in their foraging activities.

pyq.q: Name and explain the interaction between the clown fish and the sea anemone.
pyq.answer: The interaction is commensalism (+ / 0). The sea anemone has stinging tentacles and the clown fish lives among them. The clown fish benefits: it gets protection from predators, which stay away from the stinging tentacles. The sea anemone is neither benefited nor harmed; it does not appear to derive any benefit from hosting the clown fish.

pyq.q: A population of 100 Hydrilla plants in a pond produced 20 new plants in a month. Calculate the birth rate. If in the same month 5 plants died, what is the death rate?
pyq.answer:
Birth rate = births ÷ initial population = 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2 offspring per plant per month.

Death rate = deaths ÷ population = 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 individuals per plant per month.

(Net change for the month = 20 − 5 = +15 plants, so the population becomes 115, ignoring immigration and emigration.)

pyq.q: What is mutualism? Mention any two examples where the mutualistic association is commercially exploited by humans.
pyq.answer:
Mutualism is an interspecific interaction in which both the interacting species benefit (+ / +).

Examples exploited commercially: (i) Mycorrhizae, the association of fungi with the roots of higher plants, used as biofertilisers because the fungus supplies phosphorus and other nutrients to the crop while the plant supplies carbohydrates; (ii) Plant-pollinator mutualism, exploited in fruit and seed production by keeping honey bees in orchards (and in the fig-wasp system for fig cultivation). Lichens, used as dyes and indicators, are a third example.

pyq.q: Explain parasitism and co-evolution with the help of one example each.
pyq.answer:
Parasitism: an interaction in which one species, the parasite, lives on or in another species, the host, and derives its nutrition from it, harming the host (+ / −). Example: Cuscuta growing on hedge plants, which has lost its chlorophyll and leaves and draws all its nutrition from the host; ticks on dogs.

Co-evolution: the linked evolution of two interacting species. Many parasites are host-specific; if the host evolves mechanisms to reject or resist the parasite, the parasite evolves counter-mechanisms to neutralise them. Example: the orchid Ophrys and its bee pollinator; if the female bee's colour pattern changes, the orchid must change too to maintain the resemblance of its petal.

pyq.q: A koel lays its eggs in the nest of a crow. Name the interaction and explain why the crow does not throw the eggs out.
pyq.answer:
The interaction is brood parasitism, a form of parasitism in which the parasitic bird (the koel or cuckoo) lays its eggs in the nest of the host bird (the crow) and lets the host incubate them.

The crow does not eject the eggs because, in the course of evolution, the eggs of the koel have come to resemble the crow's eggs in size and colour, which reduces the chance of the host detecting the foreign eggs and throwing them out of the nest.

pyq.q: What is an age pyramid? Draw the three representative kinds of age pyramids for human populations and state what each indicates.
pyq.answer:
An age pyramid is a diagram in which the age distribution of a population (per cent individuals of each age group: pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive) is plotted, with males and females shown on the two sides for a human population. Its shape reflects the growth status of the population.

Diagram: three outlines side by side, each marked with the three age groups from base to apex.

  • (a) Expanding (growing) population: triangular, with a broad base of pre-reproductive individuals; more young are about to enter the reproductive age, so the population will grow.
  • (b) Stable population: bell-shaped, with pre-reproductive and reproductive groups nearly equal; births roughly balance deaths and the size stays constant.
  • (c) Declining population: urn-shaped, with a narrow base and a larger reproductive and post-reproductive proportion; fewer young than adults, so the population will shrink.

pyq.q: Name the two growth models that represent population growth and draw the respective growth curves they represent. State the basis for the difference in the two curves.
pyq.answer:
The two models are exponential (geometric) growth and logistic (Verhulst-Pearl) growth.

Curves: on axes of population density N against time t, the exponential curve is J-shaped, rising ever more steeply; the logistic curve is sigmoid (S-shaped), with a lag, an acceleration, a deceleration and an asymptote at the carrying capacity K, drawn as a horizontal dotted line.

Basis of the difference: the availability of resources. Exponential growth (dN/dt = rN) assumes unlimited resources, so the population realises its full innate potential to grow. Logistic growth (dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K)) assumes limited resources: the habitat can support only a maximum number K, competition for the limited resources slows growth as N approaches K, and growth stops at the carrying capacity. Because resources in nature are always finite, the logistic model is considered more realistic.

pyq.q: Describe the mutualistic relationship between the fig tree and the wasp.
pyq.answer:
Many fig species have a tight one-to-one relationship with their pollinator wasp species: a given fig can be pollinated only by its partner wasp and by no other species. The marking points:

  1. The female wasp uses the fig fruit as an oviposition (egg-laying) site.
  2. The developing wasp larvae feed on some of the developing seeds within the fruit.
  3. While searching for suitable egg-laying sites, the wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence.
  4. In return for pollination the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds as food for the larvae.

Both partners benefit (+ / +): the fig is pollinated and the wasp gets a breeding site and food for its young. The evolution of the fig and its wasp are tightly linked, an example of co-evolution of mutualists.

pyq.q: Predators play important roles in an ecosystem beyond acting as conduits of energy. Explain any three such roles with examples.
pyq.answer:
1. They keep prey populations under control. Without predators, prey species could reach very high densities and cause ecosystem instability. The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s spread over millions of hectares of rangeland and was controlled only when a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced. This is the basis of biological control of pests.

2. They maintain species diversity in a community by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species. When the starfish Pisaster was removed from an enclosed intertidal area on the American Pacific Coast, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year because of interspecific competition.
