3. They act prudently, not overexploiting their prey, since a predator that drives its prey extinct will itself go extinct for lack of food; this keeps predator and prey populations balanced over time.

pyq.q: Explain the four processes that determine the density of a population in a habitat and write the equation relating them. Under what condition does immigration become more important than natality?
pyq.answer:
The density of a population fluctuates due to four basic processes. Two increase density: natality (B), the number of births in the period added to the initial density, and immigration (I), the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere. Two decrease density: mortality (D), the number of deaths in the period, and emigration (E), the number of individuals that left the habitat.

If Nt is the density at time t, then Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Density increases when (B + I) exceeds (D + E) and decreases otherwise.

Under normal conditions births and deaths are the most important factors. Immigration becomes more significant than birth rate when a new habitat is just being colonised, since most of the individuals then arrive from outside.

pyq.q: What is competitive release? Describe the experiment that demonstrated it and state the general conclusion about which organisms competition affects most.
pyq.answer:
Competitive release is the phenomenon in which a species whose distribution is restricted to a small geographical area because of the presence of a competitively superior species expands its distributional range dramatically when the competing species is experimentally removed. It is evidence that competition occurs in nature.

Connell's field experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland: the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chathamalus from that zone. When Balanus was removed, Chathamalus spread into the intertidal zone it had been excluded from.

General conclusion: herbivores and plants appear to be more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.

pyq.q: Describe the exponential growth model of a population. Write its equation in both differential and integral forms, explain each term, name and draw the curve it produces, and state the condition under which it occurs.
pyq.answer:
Condition: exponential (geometric) growth occurs when resources (food and space) in the habitat are unlimited, so that each species can realise fully its innate potential to grow in number, as Darwin observed while developing his theory of natural selection.

Differential form: if a population of size N has per-capita birth rate b and per-capita death rate d, the change in N in unit time is dN/dt = (b − d) × N. Writing (b − d) = r, dN/dt = rN. Here r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, an important parameter for assessing the impact of any biotic or abiotic factor on population growth. Examples: Norway rat r = 0.015, flour beetle r = 0.12, human population of India in 1981 r = 0.0205.

Integral form: Nt = N0 ert, where Nt = population density after time t, N0 = population density at time zero, r = intrinsic rate of natural increase, e = base of natural logarithms (2.71828).

Curve: plotting N against t gives a J-shaped curve, starting low and rising ever more steeply without limit. Draw axes N (vertical) and t (horizontal), the curve rising like a J, and label it 'exponential growth, dN/dt = rN, resources not limiting'.

Consequence: any species growing exponentially under unlimited resources can reach enormous densities in a short time; Darwin showed how even a slow-growing animal like the elephant could reach enormous numbers in the absence of checks. Since no population in nature has unlimited resources, exponential growth cannot continue for long, and the logistic model is considered more realistic.

pyq.q: Write the Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth equation and explain each term. Draw the logistic growth curve alongside the exponential curve on the same graph, label them, and explain why the logistic model is considered more realistic.
pyq.answer:
Equation: dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), where N = population density at time t, r = intrinsic rate of natural increase, K = carrying capacity of the habitat, and dN/dt = rate of change of population density.

Carrying capacity: a habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number of a species, beyond which no further growth is possible; that limit is nature's carrying capacity (K) for the species in that habitat. The factor (K − N)/K is the unused fraction of the carrying capacity: when N is small it is nearly 1 and growth is almost exponential; as N approaches K it approaches 0 and growth stops.

Phases of the curve: a population growing with limited resources shows initially a lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when N reaches K. The plot of N against t is a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.

Graph: axes N (vertical) and t (horizontal); a horizontal dotted line labelled K; curve (a), J-shaped, rising steeply past K, labelled 'exponential growth, dN/dt = rN, resources not limiting'; curve (b), S-shaped, flattening under the K line, labelled 'logistic growth, dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), resources limiting'.

Why more realistic: no population in nature has unlimited resources. Limited resources lead to competition between individuals, and only the fittest survive and reproduce. Since resources for growth for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered the more realistic one. Governments have recognised this and introduced restraints on human population growth.

pyq.q: Explain parasitism as a population interaction. Describe the adaptations of parasites, the complexity of their life cycles with examples, the difference between ectoparasites and endoparasites with examples, and brood parasitism.
pyq.answer:
Parasitism is a + / − interaction in which the parasite lives on or in the host and derives nutrition from it, harming the host. Because the parasitic mode of life ensures free lodging and meals, it has evolved in many groups from plants to higher vertebrates. Many parasites are host-specific, and host and parasite co-evolve: when the host evolves resistance, the parasite evolves counter-mechanisms.

Adaptations: (i) loss of unnecessary sense organs; (ii) presence of adhesive organs or suckers to cling on to the host; (iii) loss of the digestive system; (iv) high reproductive capacity.

Life cycles are often complex, involving one or two intermediate hosts or vectors to reach the primary host. The human liver fluke (a trematode) needs two intermediate hosts, a snail and a fish; the malarial parasite needs a mosquito as vector.

Harm: parasites reduce the survival, growth and reproduction of the host, reduce its population density, and may make it physically weak and more vulnerable to predation.

Ectoparasites feed on the external surface of the host: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on many marine fish, and the plant Cuscuta on hedge plants, which has lost its chlorophyll and leaves. The female mosquito is not considered a parasite though it takes a blood meal. Endoparasites live inside the host body (liver, kidney, lungs, red blood cells); their life cycles are more complex because of extreme specialisation, and their morphology and anatomy are greatly simplified while their reproductive potential is emphasised.

Brood parasitism: the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them; the cuckoo (koel) and the crow. The parasite's eggs have evolved to resemble the host's in size and colour to reduce the chance of detection and ejection.

pyq.q: Explain the six types of interspecific population interactions with the help of the +, − and 0 notation. Give one NCERT example for each.
pyq.answer:
Interspecific interactions arise between populations of two different species and may be beneficial (+), detrimental (−) or neutral (0) to each. The six outcomes:

  1. Mutualism (+ / +): both species benefit. Example: lichens, a fungus with a photosynthesising alga or cyanobacterium; mycorrhizae, fungi with plant roots; fig and its pollinator wasp.
  2. Competition (− / −): both species lose; the fitness (r) of each is lower in the presence of the other. Example: Balanus and Chathamalus barnacles on the Scottish coast; flamingoes and fishes competing for zooplankton; the Abingdon tortoise and goats.
  3. Predation (+ / −): the predator benefits and the prey is harmed. Example: the starfish Pisaster preying on intertidal invertebrates; the cactus-feeding moth on prickly pear; herbivores on plants.
  4. Parasitism (+ / −): the parasite benefits and the host is harmed. Example: Cuscuta on hedge plants; ticks on dogs; the human liver fluke.
  5. Commensalism (+ / 0): one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited. Example: orchid on a mango branch; barnacles on a whale; cattle egret and cattle; clown fish and sea anemone.
  6. Amensalism (− / 0): one species is harmed and the other is unaffected. Example: bacteria inhibited by the antibiotic secreted by Penicillium.

Predation, parasitism and commensalism share a common feature: the interacting species live closely together.

pyq.q:
Study the age pyramids of two countries given below and answer the questions. Country P (Rwanda-type): a broad base, with about 40 per cent of the population in the pre-reproductive group, a smaller reproductive group and a very small post-reproductive group. Country Q (Sweden-type): pre-reproductive and reproductive groups nearly equal in size and a substantial post-reproductive group, giving a bell-like outline.
(i) Name the three age groups on which the pyramids are based.
(ii) Identify the growth status of the populations of P and Q.
(iii) Which country will need to plan for more schools and jobs in the next twenty years, and why?
(iv) Draw the age pyramid of a declining population and state one feature of its shape.
pyq.answer:
(i) Pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive age groups.

(ii) Country P has a triangular pyramid with a broad base, so its population is expanding (growing). Country Q has a bell-shaped pyramid with pre-reproductive and reproductive groups nearly equal, so its population is stable.

(iii) Country P. Its large pre-reproductive group will enter school age and then working age over the next twenty years, so it must plan for more schools and jobs; in country Q the number of young people is not increasing.

(iv) A declining population has an urn-shaped pyramid: a narrow base (few pre-reproductive individuals) with a broader reproductive and post-reproductive portion above it. Draw an outline narrow at the bottom and wider in the middle and upper part, with the three age groups labelled from base to apex.

pyq.q:
A student plotted the growth of two populations of the same species, A and B, kept under different conditions. Curve A rose ever more steeply and crossed a horizontal dotted line; curve B rose slowly at first, then rapidly, and finally flattened just below the dotted line.
(i) Which curve represents growth with unlimited food and space? Name the type of growth.
(ii) What does the dotted line represent? Define it.
(iii) Write the equation that describes curve B and name the scientists after whom this growth is named.
(iv) Which curve is more realistic for natural populations and why?
pyq.answer:
(i) Curve A, the J-shaped curve, represents growth with unlimited food and space: exponential (geometric) growth, dN/dt = rN.

(ii) The dotted line is the carrying capacity (K): the maximum number of individuals of the species that the habitat can support with its resources, beyond which no further growth is possible.

(iii) Curve B is described by dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), where N is population density at time t, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K the carrying capacity. It is called Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth.

(iv) Curve B (logistic) is more realistic, because no population in nature has unlimited resources; resources for most populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, so growth slows and stops at the carrying capacity.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. The Monarch butterfly is brightly coloured and flies slowly, yet insect-eating birds leave it alone. As a caterpillar it feeds on a poisonous milkweed and stores a chemical from the plant in its body, which makes the adult highly distasteful. In the same meadow the weed Calotropis grows untouched by the cattle and goats that graze everything around it. A survey of the meadow found 50 Monarch adults in April; by May 30 new adults had emerged and 10 had died, while 5 flew in from a neighbouring meadow and none left.
(i) Name the kind of defence shown by the Monarch and state where the chemical comes from.
(ii) Why do cattle and goats not browse on Calotropis?
(iii) Calculate the birth rate of the Monarch population for the month.
(iv) Calculate the population size at the end of May using the population equation.
pyq.answer:
(i) A chemical defence against predation: the butterfly is poisonous and distasteful to its predator (birds). It acquires the chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed; it does not make the chemical itself.

(ii) Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, a chemical defence against grazers and browsers, so cattle and goats avoid it.

(iii) Birth rate = births ÷ initial population = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6 offspring per butterfly per month.

(iv) Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) − (D + E)] = 50 + [(30 + 5) − (10 + 0)] = 50 + (35 − 10) = 50 + 25 = 75 butterflies.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is not an attribute of a population?
practice_mcq.explanation: Body weight belongs to an individual; birth rate, sex ratio and age distribution exist only for a population.

practice_mcq.q: In a pond there were 20 lotus plants last year and 8 new plants were added by reproduction. The birth rate is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Birth rate = 8 ÷ 20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year; dividing by the final population 28 is the common error.

practice_mcq.q: The shape of the age pyramid of a stable population is:
practice_mcq.explanation: A stable population has nearly equal pre-reproductive and reproductive groups, giving a bell shape; triangular is expanding and urn-shaped is declining.

practice_mcq.q: The population size of Siberian cranes at the Bharatpur wetlands in a year and of Chlamydomonas in a pond illustrate that population density in nature can range from:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: as low as fewer than 10 (Siberian cranes) or into millions (Chlamydomonas).

practice_mcq.q: Which two processes increase the density of a population?
practice_mcq.explanation: Births and immigrants add individuals; deaths and emigrants remove them.

practice_mcq.q: In the equation dN/dt = rN, r stands for:
options: Intrinsic rate of natural increase, equal to b − d

practice_mcq.explanation: Flour beetle 0.12; Norway rat 0.015; India in 1981 0.0205.

practice_mcq.q: Organisms that breed only once in their lifetime include:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT's examples of breeding once are the Pacific salmon fish and bamboo; most birds and mammals breed many times.

practice_mcq.q: Organisms that produce a large number of small-sized offspring are:
practice_mcq.explanation: Oysters and pelagic fishes produce many small offspring; birds and mammals produce few large ones.

practice_mcq.explanation: Amensalism is − / 0; commensalism is + / 0; parasitism + / −; competition − / −.

Increase the carrying capacity of prey

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is not produced by plants as a defence against grazers and browsers?
practice_mcq.explanation: Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are plant defence chemicals; Calotropis makes cardiac glycosides, not muscle protein.

practice_mcq.q: Flamingoes and resident fishes in shallow South American lakes illustrate that:
options: Competition occurs only between closely related species
Totally unrelated species can compete for the same resource
Resources must be limiting for competition
Predation is a form of competition
practice_mcq.explanation: The two unrelated groups compete for the same food, zooplankton.

practice_mcq.q: In interference competition:
options: The feeding efficiency of one species is reduced by the inhibitory presence of another even when resources are abundant
Both species increase their r value
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT uses interference competition to show that resources need not be limiting for competition to occur.

practice_mcq.q: MacArthur's study of five closely related species of warblers on the same tree demonstrated:
practice_mcq.explanation: The warblers coexisted by behavioural differences in foraging, i.e. by partitioning the resource.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these is an adaptation of parasites listed in NCERT?
options: Adhesive organs or suckers to cling to the host
practice_mcq.explanation: Parasites show loss of unnecessary sense organs, loss of the digestive system, suckers or adhesive organs, and high reproductive capacity.

practice_mcq.q: The human liver fluke completes its life cycle using two intermediate hosts, which are:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: the liver fluke, a trematode, depends on a snail and a fish as intermediate hosts.

practice_mcq.q: Cuscuta growing on a hedge plant is an example of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Cuscuta has lost chlorophyll and leaves and draws nutrition from the host, feeding on its surface; it is a parasitic plant.

practice_mcq.q: Barnacles growing on the back of a whale show:
practice_mcq.explanation: The barnacles benefit from the substrate and movement; the whale derives no apparent benefit and is not harmed.

practice_mcq.q: Lichens are a mutualistic association between:
options: A fungus and the roots of a higher plant
A fungus and a photosynthesising alga or cyanobacterium
practice_mcq.explanation: The fungus provides shelter and absorbs water and minerals; the alga or cyanobacterium photosynthesises. Fungus with roots is mycorrhiza.

practice_mcq.q: In the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys, pollination is achieved because:
options: The flower offers abundant nectar to bees
One petal resembles a female bee and the male bee pseudocopulates with it
The orchid grows on the bee's nest
The flower traps the bee until it is covered in pollen
practice_mcq.explanation: Ophrys uses sexual deceit: the petal mimics the female bee in size, colour and markings and the male is dusted with pollen while pseudocopulating.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about the fig-wasp relationship is correct?
options: Any wasp species can pollinate any fig species
The female wasp lays its eggs in the fig fruit and the larvae feed on some developing seeds
The fig is pollinated by wind and the wasp only eats the fruit
The wasp is a parasite of the fig
practice_mcq.explanation: There is a one-to-one partnership; the wasp uses the fruit as an oviposition site and pollinates the inflorescence while searching for sites, and the fig gives up some seeds as food for the larvae.

common_mistakes: Dividing by the wrong population in a birth-rate calculation. The lotus example is 8 new plants divided by the initial 20, giving 0.4; students divide by the final 28 and get 0.29, which loses the mark. Always use the population at the start of the period and write the unit (per lotus per year).

Swapping the two growth equations or the two curve names. dN/dt = rN is exponential and J-shaped; dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K) is Verhulst-Pearl logistic and sigmoid. In the graph the exponential curve crosses the dotted K line and the logistic curve flattens below it.
Calling the clown fish and sea anemone relationship mutualism. NCERT classifies it as commensalism because the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit; marking schemes follow NCERT.

Naming the interaction without saying what happens to each partner. 'Commensalism' alone for the orchid on a mango tree gets one mark; the second mark needs 'the orchid benefits, the mango is neither harmed nor benefited'.

Writing that the Monarch butterfly produces its own toxin, or that Calotropis is simply 'poisonous'. NCERT wants 'acquired during the caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed' and 'cardiac glycosides' respectively.

Confusing Balanus and Chathamalus. Balanus is the larger, competitively superior barnacle that dominates the intertidal zone; Chathamalus is the smaller one that is excluded and shows competitive release when Balanus is removed.

Stating Gause's principle without its qualification. The full answer is the principle plus 'this holds only when resources are limiting' plus 'recent studies show coexistence through resource partitioning, e.g. MacArthur's warblers'.

Drawing the age pyramids without the three age-group labels or without stating the growth status. The three shapes are worth little without 'pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive' on the axis and 'expanding, stable, declining' under each.

Preparing the deleted content. Eurythermal and stenothermal organisms, hibernation, aestivation, diapause, altitude sickness and the kangaroo rat were removed in the rationalised syllabus and are no longer asked; time spent on them is time taken from the growth models and interactions.
Treating the female mosquito as a parasite in an Assertion-Reason item. NCERT explicitly says it is not considered a parasite even though it needs a blood meal for reproduction.
strategy:
This is a short chapter in the rationalised syllabus and it is worth about 4 to 6 marks, so aim to make it a chapter where you drop nothing. Prepare it in three passes over two or three sittings.

First pass: the two growth models. Learn the exponential and logistic models as a matched pair: assumption (unlimited versus limited resources), equation (dN/dt = rN and dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K)), integral form for exponential (Nt = N0ert), curve name and shape (J and sigmoid), the four phases of the logistic curve, the meaning of r and K, the three r values, and the sentence on why logistic is more realistic. Draw the combined graph with the dotted K line from memory three times. Then do the arithmetic: the lotus birth rate, the fruit fly death rate, the doubling-time r (ln 2 divided by t) and the net-change equation with the four processes. These alone cover the 5-mark question and most 4-mark cases.

Second pass: attributes and life history. The four attributes an individual lacks, the four ways density is measured with their NCERT examples (banyan versus Parthenium, fish per trap, tiger pug marks and fecal pellets, Siberian cranes to Chlamydomonas), the three age pyramids with age groups and growth status, and the life history examples (salmon and bamboo, oysters and pelagic fish, birds and mammals) with the meaning of Darwinian fitness.

Third pass: interactions. Write the six-row +/−/0 table with two NCERT examples per row, then go through each interaction section and make a one-line card for every named example: prickly pear and the moth, Pisaster, Monarch, Calotropis, flamingoes and fishes, Abingdon tortoise, Balanus and Chathamalus, warblers, liver fluke, Cuscuta, cuckoo and crow, orchid on mango, barnacles on whale, egret and cattle, clown fish and anemone, lichen, mycorrhiza, fig and wasp, Ophrys and the bee. For each card write the interaction, who gains, who loses or is unaffected, and the one detail the examiner checks (the source of the Monarch's chemical, the two intermediate hosts, the resemblance of the cuckoo's eggs, the one-to-one fig-wasp partnership, sexual deceit and pseudocopulation).

In the exam, answer this chapter's questions in NCERT language. Where a diagram is possible (age pyramids, growth curves, the flow chart of four processes, the interaction table) draw it even if the question does not ask, because labels earn marks that prose does not. Budget about 8 minutes for a 5-mark growth-model answer, and never leave the units off a rate.
revision_checklist: I can define population and community and give the five NCERT examples of populations.
I can list the five population attributes an individual lacks and explain each in a line.
I can compute a birth rate (8/20 = 0.4 per lotus per year) and a death rate (4/40 = 0.1 per fruit fly per week) with units.
I can draw and label the three age pyramids and state the growth status each shows.
I can give four ways of measuring or estimating density with NCERT examples, including tiger pug marks and fecal pellets.
I can define natality, mortality, immigration and emigration and write N<sub>t+1</sub> = N<sub>t</sub> + [(B + I) − (D + E)], and I know when immigration matters more than births.
I can write dN/dt = rN and N<sub>t</sub> = N<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup>, define r, quote the three r values, and draw the J-shaped curve.
I can write dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K), define K, name the four phases of the sigmoid curve, draw both curves on one graph, and say why logistic is more realistic.
I can find r from a doubling time: r = ln 2 / t = 0.693 / 3 ≈ 0.231 per year for 3 years.
I can define Darwinian fitness and give the NCERT examples of breeding once versus many times and many small versus few large offspring.
I can write the six-row +/−/0 interaction table with an example for each row.
I can explain three roles of predators with the prickly pear, Pisaster and prudent-predator examples, and describe the defences of prey animals and plants.
I can state Gause's principle with its qualification, describe competitive release with Connell's barnacles, and explain resource partitioning with MacArthur's warblers.
I can list four adaptations of parasites, give the liver fluke's two intermediate hosts, distinguish ecto- and endoparasites with examples, and explain brood parasitism.
I can describe all four commensalism examples and the fig-wasp and Ophrys-bee mutualisms in NCERT's words.
